title: CAN YOUR NAME BE BLOTTED OUT OF THE BOOK OF LIFE?
paragraphs: CAN YOUR NAME BE BLOTTED OUT OF THE BOOK OF LIFE?
The terrifying question behind Revelation 3:5—and the promise of Jesus that should make every pretending Christian examine what they are trusting before eternity arrives.
There is a sentence in the Bible that can make a Christian stop breathing for a moment.
Not because it says hell exists.
Not because it says judgment is coming.
But because Jesus speaks about a name…
a book…
and the possibility of being blotted out.
Maybe you have read the verse before and hurried past it because you did not know what to do with it.
Maybe someone used it to frighten you.
Maybe someone else assured you there was absolutely nothing to think about.
But perhaps the question has followed you into quieter places:
Can someone's name actually be blotted out of the Book of Life?
And beneath that theological question may be a much more personal one.
Could it happen to me?
If you have failed God after promising Him you would change…
if you have fallen into the same sin you once wept over…
if your prayer life has become almost nonexistent…
if nobody at church knows what you have been doing privately…
if you still call yourself a Christian but somewhere inside you know your heart has grown cold…
then this is not merely an interesting question about Revelation.
It feels like your name is being discussed.
And that is why we cannot answer it with slogans.
We have to open the Scriptures.
Jesus says to the church in Sardis:
“Ὁ νικῶν… καὶ οὐ μὴ ἐξαλείψω τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ ἐκ τῆς βίβλου τῆς ζωῆς…”
Ho nikōn… kai ou mē exaleipsō to onoma autou ek tēs biblou tēs zōēs…
“The one who conquers… I will never blot his name out of the book of life…”
—Revelation 3:5
Look closely.
The Greek verb translated “blot out” is ἐξαλείψω — exaleipsō, from exaleiphō.
It carries the idea of wiping away, erasing, obliterating.
But something incredibly important appears immediately before it:
οὐ μὴ — ou mē.
Greek can express negation in several ways, but this combination gives the statement emphatic force.
Jesus is not casually saying, “I probably won't erase his name.”
He gives the conqueror a promise:
I will certainly not blot out his name.
And He does not stop there.
He says He will confess that person's name before His Father and before His angels.
Think about that.
The Christian's ultimate hope is not merely that your name survives some heavenly administrative process.
Your hope is Jesus Christ Himself.
The One who knows everything about you is the One promising to acknowledge His people before heaven.
But before turning that promise into a theological slogan, we need to hear the entire message Jesus gave Sardis.
Because Sardis had a frightening problem.
They had a reputation for being alive.
Jesus said they were dead.
Imagine that church.
People knew the songs.
They knew when to stand.
They knew Christian vocabulary.
Their reputation looked healthy enough that other people thought spiritual life was present.
But Christ saw underneath the reputation.
That means it is possible to convince people that you are spiritually alive while Jesus sees something entirely different.
And suddenly Revelation 3 is no longer about somebody else.
People who say “God is good” publicly while secretly becoming comfortable with what nailed Christ to the cross.
People who learned how to look Christian before they learned how desperately they need Christ.
Maybe nobody suspects you.
But Jesus does not examine profiles.
He examines hearts.
And His words to Sardis were not:
“Try harder to protect your image.”
They were:
Wake up.
Remember.
Keep what you received.
Repent.
That word still cuts through two thousand years of religious camouflage:
Repent.
Not perform.
Not pretend.
Not hide.
Repent.
Yet Revelation 3 is not the first place Scripture speaks about a divine book.
Centuries earlier, Israel committed catastrophic rebellion at Sinai. While Moses was with God, the people made a golden calf.
Moses then interceded for them with astonishing language:
“וְאִם־אַיִן מְחֵנִי נָא מִסִּפְרְךָ אֲשֶׁר כָּתָבְתָּ”
Ve'im-ayin, mecheni na misifrecha asher katavta.
In context:
“If not, please blot me out of your book that you have written.”
—Exodus 32:32
The Hebrew expression מְחֵנִי — mecheni comes from the verb machah, meaning to wipe out or blot out.
God answers Moses:
“Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of my book.”
—Exodus 32:33
So yes—the language of blotting someone from God's book really is biblical.
But we must not carelessly assume that every biblical reference to God's “book” describes precisely the same theological concept in precisely the same way.
Scripture uses book imagery in several contexts: divine remembrance, earthly life, judgment, and eternal life.
That distinction matters.
Psalm 69:28 speaks of names being blotted out of “the book of the living.”
Daniel 12:1 speaks of God's people being delivered, everyone found written in the book.
Jesus tells His disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven.
Paul speaks about fellow workers “whose names are in the book of life.”
And Revelation brings the imagery to its terrifying final horizon.
John sees the dead standing before God's throne.
Books are opened.
Then another book.
The Book of Life.
And Revelation 20:15 gives one of the most sobering sentences ever written:
Anyone whose name was not found written in the Book of Life was thrown into the lake of fire.
So we must not turn this subject into theological entertainment.
Eternity is involved.
But here we need humility, because faithful Christians have historically understood some of these passages differently.

Some understand Revelation 3:5 primarily as a promise of preservation: Christ is assuring genuine believers that their names will never be removed. On this reading, the verse is meant to comfort the persevering saints rather than describe genuine believers losing salvation.
Others understand the warning passages as indicating that apostasy is a genuine danger and that believers must continue in persevering faith rather than abandon Christ.
Still others distinguish between various biblical “book” passages, arguing that some refer to physical life or covenant membership while Revelation's Book of Life concerns final salvation.
We should not pretend those differences do not exist.
But something far more important can get lost while Christians fight over theological systems.
Every orthodox reading leaves you facing the same Christ.
Do not play games with Jesus.
The Bible never teaches you to stare at the Book of Life trying to discover invisible heavenly handwriting.
It tells you where to look.
Look to Christ.
Jesus said:
Notice the relationship.
They hear Him.
He knows them.
They follow Him.
He gives them eternal life.
Christian assurance is not found by saying:
“I prayed something once, therefore I can now live however I want.”
Neither is assurance found by endlessly inspecting yourself until anxiety destroys every trace of joy.

Assurance rests finally in Jesus Christ—His finished work, His promise, His grace—and genuine faith does not make peace with rebellion. The Spirit produces perseverance, repentance, obedience, and fruit in the lives of Christ's people.
Not sinless perfection.
But a new direction.
There is an enormous difference.
Peter denied Jesus.
Judas betrayed Jesus.
From a distance, both men catastrophically failed.
But their stories did not end the same way.
Peter wept.
Peter returned.
Peter was restored.
Peter discovered something every wounded believer needs to remember:
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending when Jesus Christ holds the pen.
That is the Gospel.
Not that sin is insignificant.
Sin was so serious that the Son of God was crucified.
Not that judgment is imaginary.
Christ Himself warned about judgment.
Not that repentance earns salvation.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
The Gospel is that guilty sinners who could never cleanse themselves are reconciled to God through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Christ carried sin.
Christ satisfied judgment.
Christ conquered death.
Christ rose.
And sinners who turn to Him in repentance and faith receive what they could never purchase:
forgiveness.
righteousness.
reconciliation.
life.
Maybe this is where the article stops being about “someone.”
Because you know why you clicked.
You were not merely curious about the Book of Life.
Something inside you has been afraid.
Maybe you have been wondering whether you wandered too far.
Maybe you returned to pornography after begging God to deliver you.
Maybe bitterness has been living inside you so long that it almost feels normal.
Maybe your marriage is collapsing.
Maybe you betrayed somebody.
Maybe addiction came back.
Maybe you stopped praying because every prayer felt hypocritical.
Maybe you have spent years convincing everyone else that you are okay.
And now you are wondering whether Jesus could possibly still want you.
Hear the Gospel carefully.
The invitation of Christ is not:
“Clean yourself enough to become worthy of Me.”
It is:
Come.
Come exposed.
Come guilty.
Come exhausted.
Come without excuses.
Come without pretending.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
The same Jesus who confronted deadness in Sardis also commanded that church to wake up.
Why?
Because warning itself can be mercy.
When a smoke alarm screams in the middle of the night, you do not curse it for destroying your peace.
You thank God it woke you before the fire consumed the house.
Maybe this article is an alarm.
Not condemnation telling you there is no hope.
Mercy telling you:
Wake up.
You are still hearing His Word.
Stop hiding.
Confess what you have been protecting.
Turn from what is killing you.
Run toward Christ rather than away from Him.
Because the Gospel does something scandalous.
It takes people with histories they would erase if they could…
and gives them futures they could never deserve.
The adulterer can be forgiven.
The addict can be restored.
The liar can become truthful.
The proud can be humbled.
The sexually broken can be made holy.
The religious hypocrite can finally stop performing.
The prodigal can come home.
Not because grace says sin does not matter.
Because Jesus paid a price sinners could never pay.
This is why our theme remains:
Your scandal does not shock Him.
Your hidden chapter does not surprise Him.
Your failure was not discovered by Jesus this morning.
He knew exactly what kind of sinner He was calling when He called you.
But grace is not permission to remain where He found you.
Grace rescues.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
Grace takes us toward holiness because the Savior who forgives us also becomes our Lord.
So can someone's name be blotted out of the Book of Life?
Scripture undeniably uses blotting language, and we should never erase the Bible's warnings in an attempt to make Christianity comfortable.
But Revelation 3:5 itself places a magnificent promise on the lips of Jesus:
The conqueror will not be blotted out.
The verse does not invite faithful Christians to spend their lives terrified that Jesus is standing over heaven's ledger with an eraser waiting for one bad day.
It calls the church to wake up, repent, hold fast, and overcome.
And Revelation itself tells us how God's people overcome:
through the Lamb.
Christian victory ultimately belongs to people who cling to the victorious Christ.
So perhaps the question you need tonight is not:
“Can I calculate exactly when a name could be erased?”
Perhaps it is:
Do I belong to Jesus Christ?
Not:
“Does my family think I'm Christian?”
Not:
“Was I baptized?”
Not:
Not:
“Did I once walk down an aisle?”
But:
Am I trusting Jesus Christ as Savior and Lord?
Is there repentance?
Is there faith?
When you fall, do you run toward Christ or make peace with your chains?
Do you want Jesus Himself—or merely enough religion to quiet your fear of hell?
Those questions are uncomfortable.
Let them be.
Some discomfort saves us from much greater destruction.
And if your heart is breaking because you know you have wandered, do not interpret conviction as proof that you should run farther away.
Run home.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
There is mercy at the feet of Jesus.
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is restoration for prodigals.
There is grace for the ashamed.
There is a cross for sinners.
There is an empty tomb for people who thought their story was already over.
And there is a Savior whose final word over His redeemed people is greater than the darkest word in their past.
There may be somebody scrolling tonight who would never walk into a church.
Somebody hiding an addiction.
Somebody thinking God could never forgive them.
Somebody one decision away from walking away from the faith.
But after all the Greek words…
after all the theological arguments…
after all the debates about whether a name can be blotted out…
there is something I do not want you to miss.
One day your Facebook account will disappear.
Your photographs will eventually fade.
Your possessions will belong to somebody else.
People who knew your name will themselves pass into eternity.
And when every earthly reputation has vanished, the question will not be whether people knew you as a Christian.
The question will be whether you belong to Christ.
So do not spend your life protecting a reputation while neglecting your soul.
Wake up.
Repent.
Come to Jesus.
And when shame whispers that your scandal has written the final sentence of your life, remember this:
The ink of your darkest chapter is not stronger than the blood of the Lamb.
